claims.claim: Energy efficiency is the energy service delivered compared to the energy used to produce it — output over input — so an efficient device delivers the same service using less energy.

Efficiency (same service, less energy) is distinct from conservation (less service or demand); the DOE definition frames efficiency specifically as getting the same service delivered using less energy.
Lighting efficiency is measured as luminous efficacy — light output in lumens over power input in watts — and a gas boiler's efficiency is heat output over gas input in BTUs.

The U.S. DOE lists roughly 6 to 10.5 watts of LED as delivering light equivalent to a 60-watt incandescent bulb, and ENERGY STAR-qualified lamps are required to last 10,000 hours or more (efficient models rated around 25,000 hours).

Replacing a 60 W incandescent with a 9 W LED of equal brightness run 1,095 hours/year saves about 55.8 kWh/year (65.7 kWh vs 9.9 kWh), roughly an 85 percent cut, about $8.94/year per bulb at 16 cents/kWh.

ENERGY STAR is a voluntary, government-backed labeling program administered by the U.S. EPA, established in 1992; since then it has helped avoid over $500 billion in energy costs and about 4 billion metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions.

Economy-wide energy intensity (energy used per dollar of GDP) has been declining and the EIA projects it to keep falling by roughly 1.5 percent per year through 2050, reflecting efficiency standards, incentives, and adoption of efficient technologies.
The rebound effect: when an energy service becomes cheaper to deliver, use of it tends to rise, offsetting part of the expected savings from efficiency.

William Stanley Jevons argued in The Coal Question (1865) that more efficient steam engines increased rather than decreased Britain's total coal use, because efficiency made coal-powered machinery more economical to run widely.

When the rebound effect exceeds 100 percent (total consumption rises despite efficiency), it is called the Jevons paradox or backfire; economists agree rebound is real but debate its magnitude, and widespread backfire is disputed rather than typical.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The magnitude of the rebound effect and whether full 'backfire' (Jevons paradox) commonly occurs.
positions: Some analysts argue rebound is often large and that efficiency alone cannot reliably cut total energy use.
Many environmental economists find rebound is real but usually partial, so efficiency still yields net savings; evidence for economy-wide backfire is limited.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a genuine, unresolved debate about magnitude: rebound is treated as real and worth accounting for, while backfire is described as disputed and not typical. The lesson adjudicates no policy position.
